why: Baseline single-column text PDF, ~2 pages — the simplest Tier-1 shape; must always parse cleanly.
Identical bytes to t1-pdf-single-column.pdf under an awkward filename — exercises slugifyFilename() in the recruiter upload action (src/app/(app)/candidates/[id]/actions.ts), not extraction itself.
CSS column-count:2 is the classic PDF extraction-order trap — text must still extract in reading order, column by column.

Employment-history <table>, a real <a href> hyperlink, an embedded raster image, and a running Playwright header+footer — none of that structure should confuse the extractor or leak into the body text.
The full unicode battery a real UK/EU CV can contain: diacritics, CJK, emoji+ZWJ, smart quotes, soft hyphen, an RTL fragment, an en-dash date range.
Approximates the LinkedIn "Save to PDF" export shape (bold name block, ALL-CAPS section headings, dense line breaks) that recruiters routinely upload.

Deliberately exceeds MAX_CV_TEXT_CHARS (60000, the 60k-char slice parse-cv.ts takes before calling Claude) while staying well under the 1 MiB fixture cap, proving the slice boundary itself does not corrupt or truncate mid-character.
Baseline simple DOCX with no tables/headers — must always parse cleanly, the DOCX twin of the single-column PDF.

A <w:tbl>, a real header part (word/header1.xml + its content-type + relationship), and a text box (w:txbxContent) — the DOCX structural features real CV templates use that a naive body-only reader can choke on.

Same unicode battery as t1-pdf-unicode.pdf's twin, confirming DOCX preserves RTL text in logical order (unlike the PDF, whose visual-order extraction reverses RTL presentation forms — expected PDF.js behaviour, not a bug).
Image-only PDF, no text layer — unpdf does not throw, it extracts 0 char(s); parse-cv.ts's MIN_EXTRACTED_CHARS branch (not a caught exception) is what must catch this.

Carries a syntactically valid /Encrypt dictionary with deterministic-but-not-empty-password O/U values; pdf.js's implicit empty-password check fails and throws PasswordException (observed live during generation, not predicted — research open question 4).
The first 40% of t1-pdf-single-column.pdf — no xref/trailer survives the cut, so pdf.js throws InvalidPDFException (a common real-world shape: an interrupted upload or a copy-paste truncation).
A real "%PDF-1.7" header followed by 4 KiB of deterministic (seeded) pseudo-random bytes — no valid object structure at all; pdf.js throws InvalidPDFException.
A genuinely empty (0-byte) file — the "upload never actually wrote any bytes" case; pdf.js throws InvalidPDFException.
A real, valid t1-docx-simple.docx byte-copied under a .pdf name/label — the wrong-extension case. Fed to unpdf as PDF_MIME, pdf.js throws InvalidPDFException (its magic bytes are "PK", not "%PDF").
The mirror case: a real t1-pdf-single-column.pdf byte-copied under a .docx name/label. Fed to mammoth as DOCX_MIME, jszip cannot find a central directory and throws Error.

Legacy binary .doc (OLE2 compound-file magic bytes D0 CF 11 E0 A1 B1 1A E1, not OOXML) — extractTextFromBuffer only recognises PDF_MIME/DOCX_MIME, so any real .doc mime throws UnsupportedCVMimeTypeError immediately, before any byte is even read.

Minimal {\rtf1\ansi ...} document — same mime-routing rejection (UnsupportedCVMimeTypeError) as any non-PDF/DOCX mime today; the locked "works" definition wants this said at upload time, not 3 minutes later (plan 06-08).

Mime-routing rejects this today (UnsupportedCVMimeTypeError, same as any non-PDF/DOCX mime). But its magic bytes ARE a valid ZIP — same signature as DOCX — and it is deliberately missing word/document.xml, so if it were ever mistakenly routed as DOCX_MIME, mammoth would instead throw Error ("Could not find main document part. Are you sure this is a valid .docx file?"). This is the fixture that proves a header-only magic-byte check is insufficient, which plan 06-08 depends on.
Plain text CV — same mime-routing rejection (UnsupportedCVMimeTypeError); a surprisingly common real-world upload from candidates pasting a CV into a .txt file.

A ToUnicode CMap maps glyph 0x41 ('A') to U+0000 — a real-world artefact of subset/broken font embedding. unpdf/PDF.js parses this successfully and emits 2 literal NUL byte(s) in the extracted text (verified live during generation). A green ("0 NUL") result on this fixture before plan 06-06's sanitiser ships means the FIXTURE is wrong, not the bug.

A raw 0x00 byte sits inside a <w:t xml:space="preserve"> run. mammoth reads it straight through and emits 1 literal NUL byte(s) (verified live during generation) — the DOCX twin of the ToUnicode-CMap PDF mechanism.

The XML character reference � (5 plain ASCII bytes on disk — no raw NUL byte in the file itself) resolves to a real U+0000 when mammoth's XML parser decodes it, emitting 1 literal NUL byte(s) (verified live during generation) — the second independently-verified DOCX NUL-emission mechanism.
